identifier: L. W. Tilton and J. K. Taylor, "Refractive index and dispersion of distilled water for visible radiation, at temperatures 0 to 60 degrees C", Research Paper RP1085, Journal of Research of the National Bureau of Standards 20, 419-477 (April 1938). The value entered is the 20 degC row of Table 5 (p. 446), column headed 5892.6 A, Sodium.
grade_rule: E3, grade_tag peer_reviewed. A measurement published by another laboratory: 10.3 rule 1's 'a run elsewhere is not a run here' caps it at E3 however carefully it was made. Within E3 the sort ranks peer_reviewed above vendor_spec, so this outranks a data sheet on the same quantity.
license_note: United States government work, public domain. Numeric table values and stated measurement conditions only. No text, figure or curve is reproduced.
method_as_stated: Minimum-deviation method with specially designed hollow prisms and platinum resistance thermometers, on distilled water sampled from the Bureau's still. The abstract states that all known requisites for precision and accuracy within +/-1e-6 in refractive index were employed. Observations ran from 11 May 1931 to 18 June 1934, one temperature per working day, with about five spectral lines determined per day by each of two observers. The specific conductance of the water ranged from 0.6 to 1.3e-6 reciprocal ohm-centimetre at 20 degC; one pH determination gave 6.1, described in the paper as what is expected for pure water nearly but not fully saturated with the atmosphere.
how_the_tabulated_value_was_produced: THE TABLE IS THE PAPER'S ADJUSTED RESULT, NOT A RAW READING, AND THE HEADNOTE SAYS SO. Table 5's headnote reads that the values were computed by means of the general interpolation formula (eq 3), with actual observation points shown in bold-faced type and their deviations plotted in figure 11. The abstract states the data were adjusted by least squares into a general formula of 13 constants with the average of the 133 residuals being 1.2e-6. This is the authors' own least-squares reduction of their own measurements published in the primary paper, which is a different thing from rule 5's excluded case -- a third party's fit to somebody else's data, reproduced in a database. The distinction that matters for rule 5 is who did the fitting and where it was published, not whether a fit occurred.
why_this_and_not_the_alternatives: IAPWS R9-97 (Release on the Refractive Index of Ordinary Water Substance) is the modern endorsed formulation and was obtained and read in full. It was NOT used for this entry because it is a formulation rather than a value: its Table 3 prints verification values only at 0, 100, 200 and 500 degC, none of them at bench temperature, and evaluating equation (1) at 20 degC needs a density this store does not hold, which would make the result `computed:` and therefore E4 -- worse than a printed E3 measurement, and resting on a density input carried by nothing. Daimon and Masumura, Appl. Opt. 46, 3811 (2007), is the modern measurement and is paywalled at Optica; its temperature points are 19, 21.5 and 24 degC, not 20. refractiveindex.info carries a Sellmeier fit to Daimon's data at a nominal 20 degC, which rule 5 keeps out for the same reason it kept the polystyrene fit out: the fit is somebody's model of a measurement, and evaluating it between table points is an interpolation this store may not perform. The NIST SRD reprints of Schiebener 1990 and Harvey 1998 (srd.nist.gov) returned HTTP 503 on 2026-09-20 to both the fetcher and curl.
note: READ FROM THE PRINTED TABLE AND CONFIRMED ON THE PAGE IMAGE. Table 5 prints leading digits once per column and repeats them only where they change, with an asterisk marking a value that takes its leading digits from the line BELOW. The 20 degC row sits directly under such a line, and the sodium column's leading digits change from 1.333 to 1.332 at exactly that row -- so a reader taking the tail digits 9877 under the wrong heading gets 1.3339877 instead of 1.3329877. The page was rendered at 600 dpi and the 1.332 heading was read visually above the sodium column before the value was entered. Two independent confirmations that the reading is right: the value equals the long-quoted n_D(20 degC) = 1.33299, and the F-line column at the same row reads 1.3371226 = the long-quoted 1.33712.
not_entered: The other twelve spectral lines of Table 5 at 20 degC, the same thirteen lines at the other 120 tabulated temperatures, Table 7's general interpolation table (6,776 listings on a 20 A by 1 degC grid from which the paper says sixth-decimal data may be had BY LINEAR INTERPOLATION -- which is the caller's judgement to make, not the store's), and equation 3 with its 13 constants. Any of these can be filed on request; each is a printed value and needs no interpolation as long as the wavelength and temperature asked for land on a tabulated argument.
caveat: A 1938 MEASUREMENT ON A 1938 TEMPERATURE SCALE. The temperatures are on the scale in force before ITS-90; in the 0-60 degC range the two scales differ by of order a millikelvin, which is far below anything that matters here, but the entry's 293.15 K is a conversion of the table's argument and not a claim about ITS-90. IAPWS R9-97 supersedes this paper for general use and its estimated uncertainty over 0.40-0.70 um and 5-60 degC at ambient pressure is 1.5e-5, an order of magnitude looser than this paper's stated accuracy, because the formulation spans a far wider range. DISTILLED WATER, NOT THE BUFFER. The suspension on this bench is not pure water (see particle_suspension_a); using this index for it is a substitution the caller is making.
